faq.q: What happens when you rub a balloon on your hair?
faq.a: Rubbing brings the two materials into close contact, and electrons move from your hair onto the rubber. The balloon ends up with extra electrons, and your hair with too few.

faq.q: Why is the balloon negatively charged?
faq.a: Electrons carry negative charge. Rubber holds on to electrons more strongly than hair, so it gains some, giving it an overall negative charge.
asks: Is the balloon positive or negative?

faq.q: How can a wall be attracted if it has no charge?
faq.a: The balloon's negative charge pushes the wall's electrons slightly away, leaving the surface nearest the balloon a little positive. That nearby positive patch attracts the balloon.
asks: Why does the wall pull on the balloon?

faq.a: Positive and negative charges pull on each other, while like charges push apart. The closer they are, the stronger the force, which is why the nearby positive side wins.

faq.q: Why does my hair stand up after rubbing a balloon?
faq.a: Each hair has lost electrons, so they are all positively charged. Like charges repel, so the hairs push away from each other and stand on end, and they reach towards the negative balloon.
asks: Why does static make hair stick up?

facts: The word electricity comes from the Greek word elektron, meaning amber, which attracts light objects when rubbed.
Static charge leaks away faster in damp air, so static shocks are more common in dry weather.
